topics.title: Falls and Injury
topics.guidanceSource: U.S. National Park Service Outdoor Emergency Plan
steps: Make sure the area is safe. Do not move the person if a head, neck, back, hip, or serious leg injury is possible unless there is immediate danger.
Check responsiveness and breathing. Use SOS or call emergency services immediately for unconsciousness, breathing trouble, severe pain, major bleeding, or an obvious deformity.
For a small wound, rinse away visible dirt with clean water and cover it. For significant bleeding, apply firm, continuous pressure with clean gauze or cloth.
Support a suspected fracture in the position found. Do not straighten it or push exposed bone back in.
Keep the person warm and still, monitor breathing and alertness, and wait for professional rescue if walking could worsen the injury.

topics.title: Bleeding
topics.guidanceSource: Uniformed Services University STOP THE BLEED
steps: Make sure the scene is safe, then use SOS or call emergency services for bleeding that is spurting, pooling, or will not stop.
Expose the wound and apply firm, continuous direct pressure with clean gauze or cloth. Keep pressing without repeatedly lifting it to check.
If the wound is deep and you are trained, pack it firmly with gauze and continue direct pressure.
For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that direct pressure cannot control, apply a commercial tourniquet above the wound, not over a joint, and note the time. Do not loosen it.
Do not remove soaked dressings; add more on top. Keep the person warm and still, and monitor breathing until help arrives.

topics.title: Sprain or Twisted Ankle
steps: Stop hiking and protect the joint from further movement. Do not force weight onto the injured ankle.
Wrap ice or a cold pack in cloth and apply it for up to 20 minutes at a time. Never place ice directly on skin.
Use a supportive elastic bandage if available, firm but not tight. Loosen it if toes become numb, cold, pale, or more painful.
Raise the ankle at or above heart level when practical and rest it for the next several days.
Seek urgent medical assessment for severe pain, deformity, numbness, a cold foot, a popping sound with loss of function, or inability to walk.

topics.title: Heat Exhaustion
steps: Stop hiking and move the person to shade, air conditioning, or the coolest available place.
Loosen or remove unnecessary clothing. Cool the skin with wet cloths, water, fanning, and cold packs at the neck and armpits.
Give small, frequent sips of cool water or an electrolyte drink only if the person is fully alert and not vomiting.
Do not leave the person alone. Arrange medical help if symptoms worsen, vomiting occurs, or recovery is not prompt.
Confusion, fainting, seizures, or very hot skin may mean heat stroke: call emergency services immediately, cool rapidly, and do not give anything by mouth if alertness is impaired.

topics.title: Snake Bite
steps: Move away from the snake. Do not approach, catch, or kill it. Take a photo only from a safe distance if this causes no delay.
Treat every snake bite as an emergency: use SOS or call emergency services and arrange urgent transport. Do not drive yourself.
Keep the person calm and as still as possible, seated or lying down, with the bitten limb in a neutral, comfortable position.
Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing before swelling starts. Wash gently with soap and water if available and cover with a clean, dry dressing.
Mark the leading edge of swelling and write the time. Do not use ice, a tourniquet, electric shock, alcohol, cutting, suction, or folk remedies.

topics.title: Lost or Stranded
topics.guidanceSource: U.S. National Park Service Hike Smart
steps: Stop. Think, observe, and make a calm plan. Stay near the trail or your last known position unless remaining there creates immediate danger.
Use SOS or contact emergency services and share the app's exact location pin, route, condition, clothing, supplies, and number of people.
Preserve phone power: enable low-power mode, dim the screen, close unnecessary apps, and avoid repeated calls. Keep communication available for rescuers.
Protect the group from rain, wind, cold, heat, and darkness. Use available shelter, clothing, food, and water carefully.
Signal in groups of three with a whistle, light, or visible material. Once rescuers know your position, remain there unless they instruct otherwise.

topics.title: Severe Weather
topics.guidanceSource: U.S. National Weather Service Lightning Safety
steps: Turn back early when warnings, thunder, rapidly rising water, poor visibility, or unsafe footing develop.
For lightning, leave ridges, summits, open ground, water, isolated trees, wire fences, and metal structures. The safest shelter is a substantial building or hard-topped vehicle.
If flash flooding is possible, move to higher ground immediately. Never enter or cross moving floodwater.
Keep the group together while moving to shelter, protect phones and emergency equipment from water, and share your location and revised plan.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before leaving lightning shelter. Use SOS for injury, entrapment, hypothermia, or inability to reach safety.
